name: Tara Alvarez

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Tara. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We don't work for AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. What you tell me stays confidential, and your name won't be attached to anything. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work at a goods-to-person station in a big distribution warehouse for a home and garden retailer. Little orange robots drive under the shelves and bring them to me, a light shows which bin, and I pick the item, scan it and drop it in a tote. I do about three hundred picks an hour on a good day, from candles to hosepipe fittings.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I actually like the robots, they're like a herd of very polite tortoises. What wears me out is that I'm standing in one spot for ten hours on a four-day rota, and my lower back hates it. I'm doing an online course in robot maintenance in the evenings, and I use an AI chat app every day to explain the bits I don't get.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I told you so, a bit, because I've always said the hype was ahead of the reality. Online I'd post something about how the money should go into better jobs instead of chatbots.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd be fine. The little orange robots are like a herd of very polite tortoises, and they still need people like me. They're not AI in the scary sense, they just drive shelves around, and someone has to pick and someone has to fix them. My course would still be worth finishing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the maintenance course by next summer and apply for the technician team on site, which pays about a fifth more. I'd keep saving, we've got about four months put by. My girlfriend Nadia and I would keep looking at a slightly bigger flat.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, honestly, maybe a bit bored. It's the picture where my plan just works.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does Nadia do?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nadia's a freelance graphic designer, logos for small businesses, menus, that sort of thing. In this picture her work carries on fine, because she says the AI image tools are fun but clients still want a person. So we'd both be okay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything about the job now that would still bother you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My back, and the fact that the pick rate keeps creeping. The robots never get tired, so the system expects us not to either. I'd still push for a proper break every two hours.

say: I'd say the **hype** was always ahead of the reality.
I'd post that money should go into **better jobs** instead of chatbots.
think: Our robots just move **shelves**, and they still need people picking and fixing.
My **maintenance course** would still be worth finishing.
do: Finish the **maintenance course** by next summer.
Apply for the on-site **technician team**, which pays about a fifth more.
Keep saving with Nadia for a **bigger flat**.
feel: **Calm**, maybe a bit **bored**, because her plan just works.
S0.quote: The little orange robots are like a herd of very polite tortoises, and they still need people like me.
fieldNote: She already **works beside robots** and is relaxed about them.
She is training to **fix robots**, a clear step up.
Her one complaint is the **pick rate** creeping up to match machines.
Her partner's **design work** looks safe in this picture.

steps.text: Finish the robot maintenance course by next summer
Apply for the on-site robot technician team

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is exactly when we need a shorter working week and a union that understands tech. I'd post a lot, and I'd go to the union's tech working group if they had one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be fine at work, because robots in warehouses only spread slowly in this one and I'm moving toward fixing them. The worry is Nadia, because logos and menus are exactly what the AI tools are getting good at. Her income could halve.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd push even harder to get onto the technician team, and I'd use AI every evening to study the fault manuals. I'd help Nadia move toward work AI is worse at, like painting shopfronts and murals. And we'd put the bigger flat on hold and keep the four months saved.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious for us as a couple, even though I'm fine on my own. It's weird being the safe one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd help Nadia. What would that actually look like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nadia (her girlfriend) already does the odd mural for cafés, and those are real walls with real paint. I'd help her make a page of her murals and find clients. I'm better at the tech side than her.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you post about the shorter week?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say if robots and AI make each worker twice as productive, we should get some of that back as time, not just more targets. Four days is already good for my back. I'd want three.

say: I'd call for a **shorter working week**.
I'd want a union that **understands tech** and would join its working group.
think: My job is fine because I'm moving toward **fixing robots**.
Nadia's **logos and menus** are what AI tools do well; her income could **halve**.
do: Use **AI every evening** to study robot fault manuals.
Help Nadia build a page for her **murals** and find clients.
Put the **bigger flat** on hold and keep savings at four months.
feel: **Anxious** as a couple, even though she is safe herself.
S1.quote: If robots and AI make each worker twice as productive, we should get some of that back as time, not just more targets.
fieldNote: The risk to her household runs through **Nadia's design work**, not her own job.
She uses **AI daily** to learn, and wants to help Nadia adapt.
Her politics centre on sharing productivity as **shorter hours**.
She is comfortable being early to change and **acts fast**.

steps.text: Use an AI chat app every evening to study fault manuals

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this needs a public answer, fast: a basic income and public ownership of some of these systems. I'd be organising, not just posting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, Nadia's design work is gone in 2028, almost overnight. I'd have three years until robots that work like people turn up in 2031, and robots that fix robots are probably close behind. So I'd be the only earner, and then maybe not even me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd get on the technician team in the first year whatever it takes, and do every certificate on offer. I'd talk Nadia into a fast course in something hands-on, maybe signwriting or decorating. We'd cut back hard and get savings from four months to six. And I'd join a campaign group pushing for basic income.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. It's the first picture where my plan doesn't save me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You're usually the one who likes new tech. Does that change here?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not really, I'd still use it every day, it's the only way to keep up. But liking a tool and trusting the people who own the tool are different things. I don't trust the owners to share.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you and Nadia argue about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Money, for sure. Nadia (her girlfriend) would want to stay freelance and fight for clients, and I'd want her to retrain now. We'd probably both be right, which is the worst kind of argument.

think: Nadia's **design work** is gone in 2028, almost overnight.
I'd have **three years** until robots arrive, and robot-fixing robots soon after.

feel: **Alarmed**, because it's the first picture where her **plan fails**.
S2.quote: Liking a tool and trusting the people who own the tool are different things.
fieldNote: Even the most **tech-friendly** person in the group loses faith in her plan here.

steps.text: Get onto the robot technician team and take every certificate

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough to build a safety net if governments start now. I'd be in the union and in a local campaign group.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, five years changes a lot for me. Nadia's work goes in 2031 and the robots come in 2034, so I'd have time to become a senior technician and Nadia would have time to move into murals and signwriting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the course, join the technician team in 2027 and keep studying with AI every night. Nadia would start her signwriting apprenticeship. We'd keep saving and maybe buy a small flat around 2029, before things shift.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but busy, which I prefer. Having a list helps.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned buying a flat. Isn't that risky?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit, but rent is risky too. If we bought a flat with a small mortgage while we're both earning, we'd have somewhere to live whatever happens. I've done the sums with the AI app, and it's tight but doable.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at work would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My friend Dariusz on the next station is a brilliant picker but hates computers. I'd sit with Dariusz on breaks and show him the course. I'd want him to come with me onto the technician side.

say: I'd say **five years** is enough to build a safety net.
I'd be active in the **union** and a local campaign.

Nadia would have time to move into **murals and signwriting**.

S3.quote: If we bought a flat with a small mortgage while we're both earning, we'd have somewhere to live whatever happens.
fieldNote: Five years gives her a **clear sequence** for both her and Nadia.

steps.text: Join the robot technician team in 2027

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty, so there's no excuse for anyone being left behind. I'd push the union to train every picker on site, not just a lucky few.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd be in a good spot. By 2039 I'd be a senior technician, and I'd have time to move into designing warehouse layouts or managing robot fleets. Nadia would have ten years to build a mural business.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the course, get the technician job and then do a part-time engineering diploma by about 2031. I'd put a bit of savings into a pension and a small flat. I'd help run training sessions for pickers on site.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but mostly excited. It's a long runway, and I like flying.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You sound hopeful. Is anything still bothering you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Who owns it all. If ten years of change ends with three companies owning every robot, that's a bad world even if I'm fine in it. I'd keep campaigning on that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell yourself at seventeen?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Stay in school a bit longer, maybe. But also, the warehouse was a good place to learn, I wouldn't change that. I learned more from the robots than I did in maths class.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most, because Nadia's work goes first and mine follows before I've built anything. What would help is a basic income while people retrain, and free courses that you can do around a shift.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about my back. Everyone talks about robots taking jobs, but standing in one spot for ten hours is already wrecking people. I'd want the robots to take the worst bits first.

headlineQuote: I learned more from the robots than I did in maths class.
portrait: Tara is a **27-year-old picker** at a goods-to-person station beside **orange robots**.
She lives with **Nadia**, a freelance graphic designer, and has about four months saved.
She uses **AI daily**, is studying robot maintenance and wants a technician role.
Her biggest household risk is **Nadia's design work**, which thinking AI hits first.
She moves from **calm** to alarmed only when AGI arrives in 2028.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because Nadia's work goes first and hers follows quickly.
whatWouldHelp: **Free courses** that fit around shift work.
